transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Ever since my husband’s stroke, I just haven’t been handling everything the way I usually do, and I feel like I’m not coping with all these changes. It has just been so much to adjust to all at once, and I feel very overwhelmed.
Along with feeling overwhelmed, have you lost interest in things you normally enjoy, or have you been feeling down and sad most of the day, nearly every day?

No, I wouldn't say I'm feeling down or sad most of the day, and I still care about my hobbies. It's more that I feel extremely overwhelmed and anxious, and I simply can't keep up with my usual activities and responsibilities because of all these new caregiving demands.
When did your husband have his stroke, and how soon after that did you start feeling so overwhelmed and anxious?

My husband had his stroke about six weeks ago, and we brought him home shortly after. I started feeling really overwhelmed within a week or two of having him back, once the full weight of his caregiving, medications, and appointments fell on my shoulders. It's been going on like this for about a month now.
Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms of anxiety, like trouble sleeping, muscle tension, or a racing heart, since this started?

I've definitely had trouble sleeping, often lying awake at night worrying that I'm failing my husband and letting everything fall apart. I feel constantly on edge and worn thin, but I haven't really noticed other physical symptoms like a racing heart or muscle tension. It's mostly just the exhaustion and the worry keeping me up.
Before your husband's stroke, did you often find yourself worrying excessively about various everyday things, or is this anxiety entirely new and focused only on your caregiving role?

This anxiety is completely new to me and is entirely tied to my husband's stroke and my new caregiving responsibilities. Before this, I had a very active, structured life with my church, gardening, and quilting, and I always handled my commitments well without any of this worry.

Since she has no history of chronic, generalized worry across multiple life domains and the symptoms have not persisted for the 6 months required for F41.1, GAD is ruled out. The presentation is highly consistent with an Adjustment disorder (F43.2) triggered by a major life stressor.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with emotional and behavioral symptoms (anxiety, worry, insomnia, and feeling overwhelmed) in response to an identifiable stressor (her husband's stroke and the sudden onset of heavy caregiving responsibilities). Symptoms developed within a few weeks of the stressor, have persisted for about a month, and cause significant functional impairment (inability to keep up with usual activities). Other conditions like Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) were ruled out as the anxiety is entirely new, situational, and directly tied to the caregiving role, and Major Depressive Disorder was ruled out due to the absence of depressed mood and anhedonia.
